title: The wheel and axle
prompt: A labelled teaching adaptation of the wheel-and-axle principle uses a rigid wheel fixed to a narrow rope drum on a supported shaft, with a small hanging weight. Turn wheel winds the rope and raises the weight. Drive axle applies the input at the axle and compares rim travel with axle-surface travel. Compare radii swaps between two wheel sizes while keeping the axle and load fixed. Both wheel and axle always make the same number of turns. Overlays show tangential force, travel and torque, with a larger wheel trading greater hand travel for less effort. See-through exposes the fixed shaft connection, drum, rope and supports.
blurb: A teaching winch adaptation compares wheel radii, shared turns and the trade between effort and travel.

identity.note: The Wheel and Axle chapter opens on page 30. Wheels as levers and the force versus travel diagram are on page 31 in both accessible editions.
identity.mechanism: A wheel and axle fixed together share an angle and angular speed. The larger radius travels farther per turn. Applying tangential effort at the wheel provides a greater tangential force at the smaller axle, with the corresponding travel tradeoff.
identity.classificationNote: Only The Wheel and Axle and Gears and Belts are main principle chapters in this unit. Other entries are named examples, diagrams or subsection headings. Greek Mill has both historical context and a named mechanism diagram.

prompt.note: Correction required. Turning the axle does not make a rigidly connected wheel rotate faster in revolutions per second. Its rim has greater linear speed. The bench winch is a principle adaptation, not the chapter's mammoth apparatus.
prompt.apparatusRelation: Explicit principle adaptation. A rope winch is supported by the page 31 discussion. The interchangeable wheels and measurements stage a comparison.

truthNotes: A teaching adaptation, not a reconstruction of the mammoth apparatus.
One shared angle drives wheel, shaft and drum. Rim linear travel is larger; angular speed is identical.
Ideal quasi-static torque is 0.60 Nm for a 10 N load and 6 cm drum radius. Wheel radii are 30 and 45 cm. Friction, inertia and rope thickness are omitted.
An operator supplies the inputs and holds position. No self-locking mechanism is drawn. Lower load means controlled unwinding.
Compare radii swaps a fixture while stationary; the shaft, angle, drum and load position remain unchanged.
Force arrows, radius lines and angular markers are teaching overlays, not anatomy.
1988 remains inaccessible and unverified. No edition-union completeness claim.
